stories.headline: US, EU reject UN pandemic plan
stories.title: US, EU reject UN pandemic plan
stories.summary: The United States and European Union rejected a UN declaration on pandemic preparedness, citing concerns over ideological language, intellectual property protections, technology transfers and financial commitments, while India and Germany raised reservations without opposing the proposal.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The United States and European Union rejected a UN declaration on pandemic preparedness, citing concerns over ideological language, intellectual property protections, technology transfers and financial commitments, while India and Germany raised reservations without opposing the proposal.
United Nations: The United States and the European Union have rejected a United Nations declaration intended to strengthen global cooperation against future pandemics.
However, countries like India and Germany raised concerns but stopped short of opposing the document, media reports said.
The declaration was considered on Friday during the second UN General Assembly High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response in New York.
The New York Times reported that Italy also explicitly rejected the text.
The declaration is not legally binding.
It would not dictate how governments must respond to a health emergency.
India and Germany voiced reservations about parts of the declaration but did not reject it, according to the report.
The specific objections raised by India were not detailed.
The document is expected to be sent to the General Assembly for further consideration.
The United States said the text still contained unacceptable language despite revisions made during negotiations.
Erica Schwartz, director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said it included “divisive ideologies that lack definitional consensus”.

stories.headline: A ‘superior’ CEC renders Election Commissioners ‘non-functional’, Supreme Court had warned
stories.title: A ‘superior’ CEC renders Election Commissioners ‘non-functional’, Supreme Court had warned
stories.summary: Judgement stressed collegial functioning of poll panel and said ECs must have a say in decision-making
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Nearly four decades ago, the Supreme Court had warned that if a Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) functions in a way that he considers himself superior and his word final, the Election Commissioners (ECs) would be rendered “non-functional or ornamental”.
The court had held that leaving the “exclusive and uncontrolled” powers of the Election Commission of India (ECI) in the hands of one person would violate democratic rule.

The observations of the apex court in S.S. Dhanoa versus Union of India (1991), highlighting the importance of a collegial and multi-member ECI to democracy, still echo even as allegations of unilateral conduct, authoritarianism and subversion against CEC Gyanesh Kumar highlight friction within the poll panel.

A Constitution Bench in the T.N. Seshan case, which upheld a multi-member ECI, quoted the Dhanoa judgment’s reasoning that “vast discretionary powers, with virtually no checks and balances, should not be left in the hands of a single individual and it was desirable that more than one person should be associated with the exercise of such discretionary powers”.
The court had reasoned that a single and wise individual may be able to withstand all the pulls and pressures which many may not.
However, it is politic to entrust the affairs of the ECI with more than one hand for the sole reason that the institution is armed with vast powers and is accountable to none.

The spirit of the judgment is reflected in Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, which requires the ECI to conduct its business unanimously or by the opinion of the majority consensus.
The court had said that the CEC must be able to conduct himself at meetings he chairs in a manner that he is able to win the confidence of his colleagues on the Commission and carry them with him.
On the other hand, this would prove difficult if the CEC, who is the chairman of a multi-member ECI, treats the other members of the Commission as his subordinates.
The T.N. Seshan judgment held that ECs were indeed a part of the Election Commission and “must have a say in decision-making”.
The court had at the time rejected an argument that the ECs’ role was restricted to merely tendering advice to the CEC.
The ECI is not the only multi-member body, the court had noted.

stories.headline: 'Russian crude helped India cushion oil shocks'
stories.title: 'Russian crude helped India cushion oil shocks'
stories.summary: Russian crude oil supplies enabled India to handle oil-supply delays after the conflict in West Asia disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, proving Moscow as a reliable energy partner, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko has said.Moscow could meet demand from its partners even in difficult geopolitical conditions, Rudenko recently noted. Existing arrangements between India and Russia helped “significantly mitigate” the consequences of disruptions to global energy trade, Rudenko told Russian news outlet NEWS.ru this week.Rudenko also referred to the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant built in collaboration with Russia and said another site will soon be allocated for a Russian-designed nuclear power plant.The oil refiners here increased imports of Russian crude after the US-Israeli-Iran war disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.In March 2026 following the outbreak of conflict India’s Russian crude imports nearly doubled from the previous month to 2.25 million barrels per day (bpd) and accounted for half of its oil purchases. Gulf shipments to India reportedly plunged following the war.Rudenko’s statement comes amid moves by India to raise with the USA concerns about Russia and Iran Sanctions Act threatening 100 per cent tariff for purchasing Russian oil, and after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s call for choking off Russia’s oil trade under a new US sanctions law.Russian oil shipments to India stood at about 2.1 million bpd in August, and are at around 1.9 million bpd in September, according to preliminary data from commodity analytics firm Kpler.The Indian government has maintained that securing affordable and dependable energy for its 1.4 billion people requires multiple suppliers, and warned against restrictions that could distort or constrict global energy markets.

opening: Russian crude oil supplies enabled India to handle oil-supply delays after the conflict in West Asia disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, proving Moscow as a reliable energy partner, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko has said.
Moscow could meet demand from its partners even in difficult geopolitical conditions, Rudenko recently noted.
body: Existing arrangements between India and Russia helped “significantly mitigate” the consequences of disruptions to global energy trade, Rudenko told Russian news outlet NEWS.ru this week.
Rudenko also referred to the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant built in collaboration with Russia and said another site will soon be allocated for a Russian-designed nuclear power plant.
The oil refiners here increased imports of Russian crude after the US-Israeli-Iran war disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

In March 2026 following the outbreak of conflict India’s Russian crude imports nearly doubled from the previous month to 2.25 million barrels per day (bpd) and accounted for half of its oil purchases.
Gulf shipments to India reportedly plunged following the war.

Rudenko’s statement comes amid moves by India to raise with the USA concerns about Russia and Iran Sanctions Act threatening 100 per cent tariff for purchasing Russian oil, and after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s call for choking off Russia’s oil trade under a new US sanctions law.

The Indian government has maintained that securing affordable and dependable energy for its 1.4 billion people requires multiple suppliers, and warned against restrictions that could distort or constrict global energy markets.

Rudenko’s statement comes amid moves by India to raise with the USA concerns about Russia and Iran Sanctions Act threatening 100 per cent tariff for purchasing Russian oil, and after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s call for choking off Russia’s oil trade under a new US sanctions law.

stories.headline: Saving Kashmir’s Wetlands Is Saving Our Future
stories.title: Saving Kashmir’s Wetlands Is Saving Our Future
stories.summary: Kashmir’s wetlands are often noticed only when they become scenic backdrops, birdwatching destinations or the subject of an occasional official celebration. Yet these fragile water bodies are far more than picturesque remnants of a landscape people once knew better. They are among the Valley’s most important natural systems—quietly storing floodwater, recharging groundwater, filtering pollution, supporting agriculture and sustaining a remarkable variety of birds, fish and plant life. Their decline should therefore concern every resident of Kashmir, not only environmentalists. When a wetland shrinks, is filled with debris or is cut off from its natural channels, the loss is not confined to birds and reeds. It weakens the Valley’s capacity to absorb heavy rainfall, increases the pressure on rivers and drainage networks, damages livelihoods and reduces the ecological resilience of communities already facing rapid urbanisation and a changing climate. The crisis is visible across the Valley. Wetlands have been narrowed by encroachments, fragmented by roads and construction, choked by solid waste and contaminated by untreated sewage. Water channels that once connected lakes, marshes and agricultural fields have been blocked or diverted. In several places, the boundary between wetland and settlement has become a matter of dispute rather than a clearly protected ecological limit. Each unauthorised filling may appear small, but together these interventions are eroding a system that took centuries to evolve. The consequences are particularly serious in a region vulnerable to floods. Kashmir’s wetlands function as natural sponges. During periods of intense rainfall or snowmelt, they hold excess water and release it gradually. This reduces the speed and volume of runoff entering rivers and populated areas. When these holding areas are lost, water has fewer places to go. Drains overflow more quickly, low-lying settlements face greater risk, and the burden on embankments and engineered flood-control structures increases. This natural protection is often undervalued because it does not arrive in the form of a government project or a concrete structure. But a healthy wetland can provide a service that would otherwise require expensive engineering, regular maintenance and substantial public money. Destroying such a system and then trying to replace it with pumps, walls and drains is not development. It is an expensive admission that nature was treated as disposable. Wetlands also help regulate the Valley’s water cycle. They absorb and store water, contribute to groundwater recharge and improve the quality of water by trapping sediments and absorbing some pollutants. This function becomes increasingly important as settlements expand and demand for water rises. A wetland that is polluted or disconnected from its catchment cannot perform these services effectively. Its deterioration eventually affects farms, households and downstream ecosystems. The ecological value of Kashmir’s wetlands is equally significant. The Valley lies along important migratory routes and attracts birds from distant parts of Asia and beyond. Wetlands such as Hokersar, Haigam, Shallabugh and other marshes provide feeding and resting grounds for migratory waterfowl. Their seasonal arrival is not merely a spectacle. It is evidence that these ecosystems remain connected to wider natural processes. When birds stop arriving in the same numbers, or when they find less food and shelter, the warning is ecological as well as symbolic. It indicates that water quality, vegetation, fish populations or safe resting areas may be declining. The loss of biodiversity also weakens the health of the ecosystem. Every species has a role in the food chain, nutrient cycle and regeneration of habitat. The disappearance of wetlands would also damage the Valley’s cultural memory. Kashmir’s relationship with water has always been intimate. Rivers, springs, lakes and marshes have shaped settlement, agriculture, transport, folklore and everyday life. Wetlands formed part of the seasonal rhythm of rural communities. They supported grazing, fishing, reed collection and farming. To lose them is to lose not only habitat but also a part of the landscape through which generations understood their home. Yet environmental protection in Kashmir often remains reactive. Authorities act after encroachment becomes visible, after a flood exposes a drainage failure or after public concern grows over pollution. By then, restoration is more difficult and far more costly. The priority must shift from occasional rescue to continuous protection. The first requirement is an accurate and publicly accessible inventory of wetlands. Boundaries should be mapped scientifically, updated regularly and marked clearly on the ground. Satellite imagery, local surveys and community testimony can together help identify changes in wetland area, water flow and land use. Without a reliable baseline, it is difficult to determine whether a wetland is shrinking, who is responsible or whether restoration measures are working. Legal protection must then be matched by enforcement. A wetland cannot be protected on paper while construction, dumping or land filling continues around it. Agencies responsible for revenue, planning, housing, irrigation, drainage and environment must work from the same maps and share accountability. There should be no room for contradictory permissions, delayed action or administrative ambiguity. At the same time, enforcement must distinguish between deliberate commercial encroachment and the needs of communities that have lived around wetlands for generations. People dependent on fishing, agriculture, grazing or collection of reeds should not be treated as environmental offenders by default. Conservation will succeed only when local residents see wetlands as protected commons that support their future, not as obstacles to development or threats to their livelihoods. This requires community participation in a meaningful form. Local committees can help monitor dumping, report encroachments, track changes in water levels and support seasonal protection of bird habitats. Schools and colleges can participate in wetland watch programmes, bird counts and water-quality monitoring. Such initiatives should not be reduced to ceremonial clean-up drives. They must be linked to scientific data and official decision-making. Pollution control is another urgent priority. Untreated sewage, plastic waste, agricultural runoff and construction debris are steadily reducing the capacity of wetlands to sustain life. Cleaning visible waste is useful but insufficient. The sources of pollution must be identified and controlled. Sewage treatment facilities need to function reliably, drains must be monitored and waste disposal rules must be enforced. A wetland cannot be restored if pollution continues to enter it from upstream. The wider catchment must also be considered. A wetland is not an isolated water body with a line around it. Its health depends on the streams, drains, springs, fields and slopes that feed it. If a channel is blocked or concretised upstream, the wetland may receive too little water. If soil is washed down from construction sites, it may become shallow and silted. If pesticides and sewage enter the catchment, the wetland becomes a reservoir of contamination. Restoration plans must therefore be based on hydrology rather than beautification. Removing silt may be necessary in some areas, but indiscriminate dredging can destroy vegetation and breeding grounds. Planting ornamental species along a wetland edge may improve its appearance while harming its ecological character. Concrete walkways, lighting and commercial facilities can fragment habitat and disturb birds. A restored wetland should be judged by its ecological function, not by how attractive it looks in a photograph. Urban planning must also change. The Valley’s towns are expanding rapidly, often into low-lying and water-sensitive areas. Master plans should identify wetlands, floodplains and natural drainage channels as no-build zones. Roads and housing projects must be assessed for their impact on water flow before construction begins. Development cannot be called sustainable if it creates flood risk for the very communities it is meant to serve. Climate change makes this task even more urgent. Changes in rainfall patterns, warmer winters, irregular snowfall and intense precipitation events are already altering the Valley’s hydrology. Wetlands provide a buffer against such uncertainty. They cannot prevent every flood or drought, but they can reduce vulnerability. Protecting them is therefore an essential part of climate adaptation, not a luxury reserved for times when other problems have been solved. The economic argument for conservation is strong as well. Wetlands support agriculture, fisheries, tourism, research and local employment. They reduce the cost of flood damage, water treatment and artificial drainage. Bird tourism, if managed responsibly, can create income for surrounding communities without destroying habitat. But economic use must remain within ecological limits. A wetland that is overbuilt, overvisited or polluted will eventually lose the very qualities that attract visitors and generate income. What is needed now is not another declaration of concern but a Valley-wide wetland action plan with clear targets, timelines and responsibility. It should identify priority wetlands, publish their boundaries, measure water quality, restore natural channels, remove major pollution sources and establish a transparent system for reporting violations. Progress should be reviewed publicly, and local communities should have access to the information. The government has an important role, but responsibility does not end there. Citizens must stop treating wetlands as dumping grounds or vacant land. Builders and businesses must recognise that short-term gains from illegal filling impose long-term costs on society. Political representatives must resist the temptation to support encroachments for immediate popularity. Courts, civil society, researchers and the media must continue to draw attention to violations and demand accountability. Kashmir’s wetlands are not empty spaces waiting to be converted. They are living infrastructure, natural archives and shared inheritance. They protect towns, nourish fields, host migratory birds and preserve the ecological balance of the Valley. Once destroyed, they cannot be recreated simply by digging a new pond or planting a few saplings. The choice before Kashmir is clear. It can continue to allow wetlands to disappear through gradual neglect, fragmented permissions and weak enforcement, or it can treat them as essential public assets deserving serious investment and protection. Saving them will require patience, science, law and community participation. But the cost of inaction will be far greater. To save the wetlands is to save the Valley’s water, biodiversity, memories and future. That is not an environmental slogan. It is a public necessity. (The author is a research scholar and freelancer)
